title: 6.3 — ANOVA Decomposition and the Overall F Test
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.3 ANOVA decomposition and overall F test
engineName: Decompose total variation into explained and residual parts, then derive the overall regression F test and its expression through R².
objectives: Derive the corrected-total sum-of-squares decomposition for regression with an intercept.
Construct the regression ANOVA table and identify degrees of freedom and mean squares.
Derive the overall F statistic for testing all slope coefficients jointly.
Express the overall F statistic in terms of R², n and k.
Distinguish the overall F test from individual t tests and partial F tests.
Interpret numerator and denominator degrees of freedom correctly.

prereq.name: OLS fitted values and residuals
prereq.why: ANOVA separates the fitted component from the residual component.

prereq.name: Hat and residual-maker matrices
prereq.why: Orthogonal projections explain why the sums of squares add.

prereq.name: F distribution and degrees of freedom
prereq.why: The test statistic is a ratio of independent mean squares under the null.

traps: Use k as the total number of estimated parameters including the intercept; the number of tested slopes is k−1.
For the overall regression test, numerator df=k−1 and denominator df=n−k.
The overall F test tests all slope coefficients jointly; it is not the same as testing one coefficient with a t statistic.
In simple linear regression with one slope, overall F equals the square of the slope t statistic.
Corrected TSS=RegSS+RSS for OLS with an intercept.
Adding a predictor cannot increase RSS in nested OLS and cannot decrease R²; adjusted R² may move either way.
A large F is evidence against the joint null, not proof of causality or correct specification.
howto: Identify n and k (including intercept); compute RegSS and RSS or R²; divide each sum of squares by its df; form F=MSR/MSE; compare with F critical or p-value; for an R²-only question substitute the compact formula.

provenance: Direct anchor: June 2026 UGC NET Statistics Paper 2 Q9 (j26-q09). Official key B; response sheet Q114 records the learner marked A. The stem asks for the F statistic for significance of complete regression excluding the intercept. The printed expression is normalized as F=[R²/(k−1)]/[(1−R²)/(n−k)], with k the total number of parameters including the intercept. The ten linked variants form a mixed cluster: ANOVA/F, adjusted R², multicollinearity and residual variance. Only relevant F/ANOVA variants are treated as related practice.

sheet: Corrected TSS=Σ(yᵢ−ȳ)²=RegSS+RSS for OLS with an intercept.
Regression df=k−1; residual df=n−k; total df=n−1.
Under H₀ and classical normal-error assumptions, F follows F(k−1,n−k).
For one slope, F=t² for the same coefficient test.
A significant overall F means at least one slope is nonzero; it does not identify which one.
Nested OLS: RSS cannot increase and R² cannot decrease when predictors are added; adjusted R² can.
tricks: If given R², n and k, use the compact formula directly.
If an ANOVA table gives sums of squares and df, compute mean squares first, then divide.
Check denominator df: n−k, not n−1.
For simple regression, overall F and slope t are linked by F=t².
shortcuts: Overall regression test = all slopes jointly zero.
Numerator df = number of slopes; denominator df = residual df.
The compact R² formula is a ratio of explained proportion per slope df to unexplained proportion per residual df.
remember: The conventional ANOVA decomposition and compact R² formula assume an intercept and ordinary least squares.
If k is defined as predictors excluding the intercept, use numerator df=k and denominator df=n−k−1.

scenes.title: Refresh variation and degrees of freedom
scenes.objective: Recover the ingredients used in a regression ANOVA table.
body: ANOVA compares variation explained by the fitted model with variation left in residuals. Before calculating F, make sure the three sums of squares and their degrees of freedom are clear.
This lesson uses k for the total number of estimated parameters, including the intercept. Therefore k−1 slope coefficients are tested in the overall regression test.

items.ask: What does the sample mean represent in corrected total sum of squares?
items.recall: The reference value around which response variation is measured.
refresh: Corrected total variation measures deviations from the sample mean: TSS=Σ(yᵢ−ȳ)².
The mean is the natural baseline for a model containing an intercept.
The total degrees of freedom are n−1 because one degree of freedom is used in estimating the sample mean.

items.ask: If a model has k parameters including the intercept, how many slopes does it have?
refresh: The intercept is one of the k parameters in the model. The other k−1 parameters are slopes attached to explanatory variables.
The overall regression test asks whether all of those slope coefficients are zero at the same time. This is a joint hypothesis with k−1 restrictions.
That is why the numerator degrees of freedom are k−1. If a question instead defines k as the number of predictors excluding the intercept, its numerator df is k and the residual df is n−k−1.
Always read the question's definition of k before substituting. This lesson consistently counts the intercept inside k.

items.recall: A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom.
refresh: A sum of squares measures variation on a squared scale.
Dividing by the corresponding degrees of freedom produces a mean square.
The overall F statistic is the regression mean square divided by the residual mean square.

ask.q: If k counts all parameters including the intercept, how many slope restrictions are in the overall test?

scenes.title: Explained variation and leftover variation
body: The fitted values are the model's projection of y onto the column space of X. Residuals are the part left after that projection.
With an intercept, fitted deviations from the sample mean and residuals are orthogonal. Their squared lengths add: TSS=RegSS+RSS.
The overall F test asks whether explained variation per fitted slope is large relative to unexplained variation per residual degree of freedom.

scenario.teaser: A regression model partitions response variation
scenario.title: Where did the variation go?
body: A response variable varies around its sample mean. Regression explains some of that variation through fitted values.
The explained component is RegSS. The unexplained component is RSS. For OLS with an intercept, these components are orthogonal and add to corrected TSS.
If the model explains little relative to residual noise, F tends to be small. If it explains a substantial amount relative to residual variation, F tends to be large.
The test evaluates the joint contribution of all slope terms, not one selected predictor.
scenario.q: Which two components add to corrected total sum of squares?
scenario.answer: Regression sum of squares and residual sum of squares.

ask.q: What does the overall F test compare?
ask.nudge: Think of explained and unexplained mean squares.

scenes.title: Derive the sums-of-squares decomposition
body: Write y−ȳ1=(ŷ−ȳ1)+e. The first term is the fitted deviation from the mean; the second is the residual vector.
OLS residuals are orthogonal to the fitted space. With an intercept, e is also orthogonal to the constant vector, so e′(ŷ−ȳ1)=0.
Taking squared lengths gives (y−ȳ1)′(y−ȳ1)=(ŷ−ȳ1)′(ŷ−ȳ1)+e′e. This is TSS=RegSS+RSS.

viz.caption: Orthogonal fitted and residual components give an additive sum-of-squares decomposition.

ask.q: Which cross-product disappears when the squared norm is expanded?
ask.nudge: It is twice the inner product between fitted deviations and residuals.

scenes.title: Build the regression ANOVA table
scenes.objective: Identify sums of squares, degrees of freedom and mean squares.

blocks.body: Regression: k−1. Residual: n−k. Total: n−1. The two component degrees of freedom add to n−1.
The overall regression statistic is F=MSR/MSE. Under the joint null and classical normal-error assumptions, it has an F distribution with (k−1,n−k) degrees of freedom.

ask.q: For n=40 and k=5, what are regression and residual degrees of freedom?
ask.nudge: The numerator uses the number of slopes; the denominator uses n minus all parameters.

scenes.title: Worked example: calculate F from an ANOVA table
scenes.objective: Compute mean squares and their ratio.
scenes.problem: An ANOVA table reports RegSS=66,870 with 3 df and RSS=5,344 with 16 df. Find F.

steps.why: Divide regression sum of squares by its 3 degrees of freedom.
Divide residual sum of squares by its 16 degrees of freedom.
The overall test compares explained mean square with residual mean square.
A large ratio is evidence against the joint null, subject to model assumptions.

ask.q: Why divide each sum of squares before taking the ratio?
ask.nudge: F compares mean squares, not raw sums of squares.

scenes.title: Derive F from R²
scenes.objective: Express the overall F test using R², n and k.

blocks.body: R²=RegSS/TSS and 1−R²=RSS/TSS. Hence RegSS=R²·TSS and RSS=(1−R²)·TSS.
Here k includes the intercept. If a question defines k as predictors excluding the intercept, equivalent df are k and n−k−1.

ask.q: What is denominator df in the stated convention?
ask.nudge: Subtract total estimated parameters from n.

scenario.teaser: A formula can be reconstructed from its two mean squares
scenario.title: From R² to an F statistic
body: Suppose the output gives R² but not the raw sums of squares. You can still reconstruct the overall F ratio because R² is the explained fraction of total variation.
The unexplained fraction is 1−R². Divide the explained fraction by the number of tested slopes, and divide the unexplained fraction by residual degrees of freedom.
Taking the first quantity divided by the second gives the same F statistic as the ANOVA table. This is the algebraic shortcut used in the official June 2026 Q9.
scenario.q: Why does total sum of squares disappear from the compact formula?
scenario.answer: It appears in both RegSS=R²·TSS and RSS=(1−R²)·TSS, so it cancels in their ratio.

scenes.objective: Apply the compact expression and keep df consistent.
scenes.problem: A regression has n=50, k=5 total parameters including intercept, and R²=0.55. Calculate F.

steps.why: There are four slopes and 45 residual degrees of freedom.

steps.say: Calculate explained proportion per regression df.
steps.why: The explained proportion is spread over four tested slopes.

steps.say: Calculate unexplained proportion per residual df.
steps.why: The unexplained proportion is divided by residual df.
This is the overall F statistic for all four slopes jointly.

ask.q: If R² increases while n and k stay fixed, what happens to F?
ask.nudge: The numerator rises and the denominator falls.

scenes.title: Overall F versus individual t tests

blocks.body: H₀:β₂=β₃=…=βₖ=0. The alternative is that at least one slope is nonzero.
A t test examines one coefficient at a time. The overall F test assesses the joint contribution of all slopes.
With one slope, the overall F test and two-sided t test for that slope are equivalent: F=t².
A significant overall F does not prove every slope is significant. It indicates that the full set of slopes is jointly informative under the model assumptions.

ask.q: If overall F is significant, must every individual t test be significant?
ask.nudge: The overall test says at least one slope contributes, not all.

scenes.title: Guided problem: read the ANOVA table
scenes.objective: Interpret the test and its degrees of freedom.
scenes.problem: A regression ANOVA table has regression df=2, residual df=27, MSR=48 and MSE=4. Find F and state the joint null.
hints: The two df values identify the F distribution.
The overall null sets all slope coefficients equal to zero.
scenes.answer: F=12; reference distribution F(2,27). The null is that both slopes are zero jointly.

solution.math: The test evaluates both slopes jointly.

ask.q: What does numerator df=2 tell you?
ask.nudge: It counts the slope restrictions tested.

scenes.title: Exam traps: ANOVA and R²
scenes.objective: Catch common errors in the F formula.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: When k includes the intercept, overall regression numerator df is k−1.

items.why: It is n−k when k parameters are estimated.

items.claim: The overall F statistic is MSR divided by MSE.
items.why: This is the ratio of regression and residual mean squares.
The expression is a ratio, not a product.

items.claim: A significant overall F proves all slopes are individually significant.
items.why: It establishes joint significance of at least one slope.

scenes.title: Model changes and adjusted R²
scenes.objective: Separate ordinary R² behaviour from adjusted R².

blocks.body: For nested OLS models, adding a predictor cannot increase RSS. Therefore ordinary R² cannot decrease.
Adjusted R²=1−[(RSS/(n−k))/(TSS/(n−1))], with k total parameters including intercept.
Adjusted R² penalizes model complexity. It can increase or decrease when a predictor is added, unlike ordinary R².
Adjusted R² is a model-comparison measure; it is not the overall F statistic.

ask.q: Can adjusted R² decrease when a predictor is added?
ask.nudge: It includes a penalty for spending an additional parameter.

scenes.title: Summary: regression ANOVA and F
scenes.objective: Retain decomposition, df and compact F formula.
body: For OLS with an intercept, corrected TSS=RegSS+RSS. ANOVA uses regression df=k−1, residual df=n−k and total df=n−1, where k includes the intercept.
MSR=RegSS/(k−1), MSE=RSS/(n−k), and F=MSR/MSE. For the joint null that all slopes are zero, F follows F(k−1,n−k) under classical normal-error assumptions.
Since R²=RegSS/TSS and 1−R²=RSS/TSS, F=[R²/(k−1)]/[(1−R²)/(n−k)]. The overall F test is joint; it does not imply every individual t test is significant.

ask.q: State the compact F formula and define k.
